cards.hypothesis: Subject-level variation in wearable stress-detection uncertainty is driven by individual differences in baseline autonomic tone, specifically resting heart rate variability (HRV), which influences algorithm calibration accuracy.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Higher resting HRV improves the calibration of the stress detection algorithm, reducing predictive uncertainty.
cards.causal_path: Baseline HRV → algorithm calibration accuracy → stress-detection uncertainty
cards.rival_explanation: Variation in uncertainty is primarily due to inconsistencies in sensor placement across subjects.
cards.rival_prediction: Subjects with poorer placement consistency will show higher uncertainty regardless of their baseline HRV.
cards.distinguishing_test: After statistically controlling for placement variability (e.g., using accelerometer-derived placement metrics), baseline HRV remains a significant predictor of uncertainty.
cards.effect_size_rationale: Prior studies report moderate correlations (r≈0.3) between resting HRV and stress classification performance.
cards.testable_prediction: Subjects with higher baseline HRV will exhibit lower uncertainty scores (negative association).
cards.failure_condition: No significant negative association between baseline HRV and uncertainty after adjusting for age, VO2max, and beta‑blocker use.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Linear mixed‑effects model with uncertainty as the outcome, baseline HRV as a fixed effect, random intercept for subject, and age, VO2max, beta‑blocker use as covariates.
cards.falsification_test: Induce a transient change in resting HRV via paced breathing while holding placement constant; if uncertainty does not change in the predicted direction, the mechanism is falsified.

cards.hypothesis: Individual differences in skin impedance affect PPG signal quality, leading to subject‑level variation in stress‑detection uncertainty.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Higher skin impedance reduces PPG signal‑to‑noise ratio, which increases the uncertainty of the stress detection model.
cards.rival_explanation: Uncertainty differences are mainly caused by non‑individualized algorithm threshold settings.
cards.rival_prediction: If thresholds are individualized per subject, skin impedance will no longer predict uncertainty.
cards.distinguishing_test: Compare uncertainty before and after applying individualized thresholds; a persistent effect of skin impedance after threshold adjustment supports the mechanism.
cards.effect_size_rationale: Skin impedance can vary by >10 kΩ across individuals, producing >10 dB changes in PPG SNR, which prior work links to large shifts in detection error.
cards.testable_prediction: Higher skin impedance predicts higher uncertainty (positive association).
cards.failure_condition: No significant positive association between skin impedance and uncertainty after controlling for sweat, motion, and temperature.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Multiple regression of uncertainty on skin impedance with sweat rate, accelerometer variance, and ambient temperature as covariates.
cards.falsification_test: Temporarily lower skin impedance using a conductive gel; if uncertainty does not decrease accordingly, the mechanism is falsified.

cards.hypothesis: Variability in the latency of the cortisol stress response creates misalignment between self‑report stress labels and wearable physiological signals, increasing uncertainty.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Slower cortisol peaks cause temporal mismatch between label timestamps and model‑expected stress signatures, raising uncertainty.
cards.rival_explanation: Uncertainty stems mainly from inconsistent self‑report compliance rather than hormonal timing.
cards.rival_prediction: Subjects with low compliance will show high uncertainty irrespective of cortisol latency.
cards.distinguishing_test: After adjusting for self‑report compliance scores, cortisol latency remains a significant predictor of uncertainty.
cards.effect_size_rationale: Earlier work shows moderate correlations (r≈0.35) between hormonal response latency and self‑report physiological alignment.
cards.testable_prediction: Longer cortisol latency predicts higher uncertainty (positive association).
cards.failure_condition: No significant positive association between cortisol latency and uncertainty after controlling for compliance, time of day, fasting, and stressor type.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Linear mixed‑effects model with uncertainty as outcome, cortisol latency as fixed effect, random subject intercept, and compliance, time of day, fasting, stressor type as covariates.
cards.falsification_test: Administer a CRH agonist to advance cortisol response; if uncertainty does not decrease as predicted, the mechanism is falsified.

cards.hypothesis: Individual circadian phase influences baseline drift of electrodermal activity (EDA), producing time‑of‑day dependent variation in stress‑detection uncertainty.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Circadian‑dependent EDA baseline drift alters the background against which stress‑related changes are detected, increasing uncertainty when drift is large.
cards.rival_explanation: Uncertainty fluctuations are driven primarily by battery voltage decline over the recording session.
cards.rival_prediction: Lower battery voltage predicts higher uncertainty independent of circadian phase.
cards.distinguishing_test: After statistically controlling for battery level, circadian phase still predicts uncertainty.
cards.effect_size_rationale: Prior work shows modest but significant circadian modulation of EDA baseline (≈5‑10 % amplitude).
cards.testable_prediction: Uncertainty is higher during the biological night (circadian phase 0‑6 h) for individuals with delayed phase.
cards.failure_condition: No significant interaction between circadian phase and uncertainty after adjusting for battery, sleep, caffeine, and activity.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Linear mixed‑effects model with uncertainty as outcome, circadian phase, battery level, and their interaction as fixed effects, random intercept for subject, and sleep, caffeine, activity as covariates.
cards.falsification_test: Conduct a constant‑routine protocol to eliminate circadian variation; if uncertainty still varies with clock time, the mechanism is falsified.

cards.hypothesis: Individual differences in alexithymia increase noise in self‑report stress labels, which propagates to higher model uncertainty.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Greater alexithymia reduces the reliability of subjective stress reports, inflating label noise and thus the uncertainty of the learned stress detector.
cards.rival_explanation: Uncertainty differences arise mainly from variations in stressor intensity across subjects.
cards.rival_prediction: Higher variability in administered stressor intensity leads to higher uncertainty regardless of alexithymia.
cards.distinguishing_test: After controlling for stressor‑intensity variance, alexithymia remains a significant predictor of uncertainty.
cards.effect_size_rationale: Studies report moderate associations (r≈0.3) between alexithymia and self‑report reliability.
cards.testable_prediction: Higher alexithymia predicts higher uncertainty (positive association).
cards.failure_condition: No significant positive association between alexithymia and uncertainty after adjusting for education, language proficiency, and mood disorder.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Regression of uncertainty on alexithymia with years of education, TOEFL score, and PHQ‑9 as covariates.
cards.falsification_test: Replace self‑report labels with objective biomarker labels (e.g., cortisol) and retrain the model; if uncertainty no longer correlates with alexithymia, the mechanism is supported; if the correlation persists, it is falsified.

cards.hypothesis: Unmodeled hypertensive subpopulations produce heteroscedastic uncertainty because altered vascular tone changes PPG amplitude and degrades model fit for those subjects.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Hypertension‑related vascular tone shifts reduce PPG pulse amplitude, increasing model residuals and thus uncertainty for hypertensive individuals.
cards.rival_explanation: Uncertainty differences are primarily due to differing physical activity levels between hypertensive and normotensive subjects.
cards.rival_prediction: After adjusting for activity, hypertension status no longer predicts uncertainty.
cards.distinguishing_test: Include physical activity as a covariate; if hypertension remains a significant predictor, the mechanism is supported.
cards.effect_size_rationale: No prior work has quantified the uncertainty gap between hypertensive and normotensive wearables; variance‑components analysis is needed.
cards.testable_prediction: Hypertensive subjects exhibit higher uncertainty than normotensive subjects (positive direction).
cards.failure_condition: No significant difference in uncertainty between hypertensive and normotensive groups after controlling for medication, arterial stiffness, age, and activity.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Linear mixed‑effects model with uncertainty as outcome, hypertension as fixed effect, random subject intercept, and medication, pulse wave velocity, age, activity as covariates.
cards.falsification_test: Train separate stress‑detection models for hypertensive and normotensive subsamples; if the uncertainty gap disappears when models are group‑specific, the mechanism is supported; if the gap persists, it is falsified.

cards.hypothesis: Subjects whose feature vectors lie far from the training distribution incur higher model‑based uncertainty due to extrapolation.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Greater Mahalanobis distance from the training feature distribution signals out‑of‑domain inputs, which Bayesian or ensemble models interpret as higher predictive uncertainty.
cards.rival_explanation: Uncertainty differences arise mainly from disagreement among ensemble members unrelated to input distance.
cards.rival_prediction: High ensemble variance can occur even for in‑distribution points, producing uncertainty unrelated to Mahalanobis distance.
cards.distinguishing_test: After accounting for ensemble variance, Mahalanobis distance still predicts uncertainty.
cards.effect_size_rationale: Out‑of‑distribution samples routinely increase predictive uncertainty by factors of 2 or more in deep ensembles.
cards.testable_prediction: Larger Mahalanobis distance predicts higher uncertainty (positive association).
cards.failure_condition: No significant positive association between Mahalanobis distance and uncertainty after controlling for scaling and imputation method.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Linear mixed‑effects model with uncertainty as outcome, Mahalanobis distance as fixed effect, random intercept for subject, and scaling technique and imputation approach as covariates.
cards.falsification_test: Project out‑of‑distribution samples back into the training subspace via PCA reconstruction; if uncertainty does not decrease after projection, the mechanism is falsified.

cards.hypothesis: Subject‑specific motion artifact levels corrupt wearable features, increasing uncertainty in stress detection.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Higher motion introduces spurious variations in PPG and EDA channels, which the model interprets as stress‑related signal, raising predictive uncertainty.
cards.rival_explanation: Uncertainty differences are mainly due to variations in individual stress reactivity rather than motion.
cards.rival_prediction: Subjects with high intrinsic stress reactivity will show high uncertainty even when motion is low.
cards.distinguishing_test: After controlling for a physiological stress reactivity index (e.g., task‑evoked HRV change), motion artifact level still predicts uncertainty.
cards.effect_size_rationale: Prior work shows moderate effect sizes (Cohen’s d≈0.5) of motion artifact on PPG signal quality.
cards.testable_prediction: Higher motion artifact level predicts higher uncertainty (positive association).
cards.failure_condition: No significant positive association between accelerometer variance and uncertainty after adjusting for melanin index, strap tension, ambient vibration, and stress reactivity.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Multiple regression of uncertainty on accelerometer variance with melanin index, strap tension, ambient vibration, and task‑evoked HRV change as covariates.
cards.falsification_test: Constrain subject movement using a rigid harness while preserving physiological stress induction; if uncertainty does not drop accordingly, the mechanism is falsified.

cards.hypothesis: Individual differences in sleep inertia cause systematic delays in self‑report stress labeling, increasing label‑time misalignment and model uncertainty.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Upon waking, slowed cognitive processing delays self‑report entry, shifting labels relative to physiological stress onset and inflating uncertainty.
cards.rival_explanation: Uncertainty differences arise mainly from random variability in self‑report compliance unrelated to sleep state.
cards.rival_prediction: Low compliance predicts high uncertainty irrespective of sleep inertia duration.
cards.distinguishing_test: After adjusting for compliance scores, sleep inertia duration remains a significant predictor of uncertainty.
cards.effect_size_rationale: Sleep inertia effects on cognitive performance are typically small to moderate (effect size ≈0.3).
cards.testable_prediction: Longer sleep inertia predicts higher uncertainty (positive association).
cards.failure_condition: No significant positive association between sleep inertia duration and uncertainty after controlling for compliance, total sleep, caffeine, and minutes since wake.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Linear mixed‑effects model with uncertainty as outcome, sleep inertia as fixed effect, random subject intercept, and compliance, total sleep, caffeine, minutes since wake as covariates.
cards.falsification_test: Administer a short nap protocol that eliminates sleep inertia; if uncertainty does not decrease for post‑nap reports, the mechanism is falsified.

cards.hypothesis: Failure to model within‑subject temporal autocorrelation leads to underestimated uncertainty for subjects with high intra‑individual variability.
cards.proposed_mechanism: Ignoring autocorrelation causes the model to treat correlated observations as independent, producing overly confident predictions and thus lower reported uncertainty for stable subjects, while high‑variability subjects show higher observed uncertainty.
cards.rival_explanation: Uncertainty differences are mainly due to true differences in underlying stress volatility across subjects.
cards.rival_prediction: Subjects with genuinely higher stress volatility will have higher uncertainty even when autocorrelation is properly modeled.
cards.distinguishing_test: Fit two models: one ignoring autocorrelation, one with an AR(1) residual structure; if the autocorrelation‑aware model reduces the uncertainty gap between high‑ and low‑variability subjects, the mechanism is supported.
cards.effect_size_rationale: The magnitude of bias from ignoring autocorrelation depends on the intra‑class correlation coefficient, which must be estimated from data.
cards.testable_prediction: Subjects with higher lag‑1 autocorrelation will show larger discrepancy between reported uncertainty and observed error variance (positive association).
cards.failure_condition: No significant positive association between autocorrelation lag‑1 and the difference between observed error variance and reported uncertainty after controlling for observation count, sampling rate, and experimenter.
cards.statistical_test_plan: Regression of (observed_error_variance − reported_uncertainty) on lag‑1 autocorrelation with observation count, sampling rate, and experimenter ID as covariates.
cards.falsification_test: Re‑fit the stress‑detection model using a mixed‑effects framework that explicitly models subject‑level autocorrelation; if the uncertainty‑variance discrepancy disappears, the mechanism is supported; if it persists, the mechanism is falsified.
